questions.q: What is a privacy impact assessment (PIA)?
options: A technical scan that automatically encrypts all personal data in a system
A review performed only after a confirmed data breach has occurred
A structured review of a planned data processing activity's privacy risks, done before it launches
A quarterly access recertification report
questions.explain: A PIA is a pre-launch, forward-looking review — it's done before a system touches personal data, to identify and address risks in advance rather than after an incident.

questions.q: Under GDPR Article 35, when is a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) specifically required?
options: For every single project that touches any personal data, with no exceptions
Only when a breach has already occurred
Only after a data subject request has been received
When processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, such as large-scale sensitive data processing or systematic monitoring
questions.explain: Article 35 ties the formal DPIA requirement to processing that is likely to pose a high risk to individuals, citing large-scale sensitive data processing and systematic monitoring as examples.

questions.q: What does the 'necessity and proportionality' question in a PIA actually test?
options: Whether the data has already been classified
Whether the project has a signed contract with a data processor
Whether the same purpose could be achieved with less data or a less invasive approach
Whether the organization has enough storage capacity for the data
questions.explain: This question applies the minimization principle before the system exists, asking whether less data or a less invasive method could achieve the same purpose.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how would a PIA have changed the outcome of the Brightfield dashboard project from Lesson 28?
options: It would have surfaced that the dashboard only needed aggregated regional totals and flagged the broad access grant before launch, rather than relying on recertification to catch it months later
It would have automatically revoked the contractor's access without human review
It would have had no effect, since PIAs only apply after an incident
It would have replaced the need for an access governance model entirely
questions.explain: Running the project through a PIA's 'what data and why' and 'necessary and proportionate' questions would have caught the mismatch between the dashboard's actual needs and the broad access granted, at design time instead of three months later.
